vignette:
He is 40, a Middle Eastern man who has spent most of his adult life moving toward emergencies while other people step back. As a paramedic, he is used to blood, shouting, the metallic smell of accident scenes, and the ritual of staying calm when others cannot. For years he takes pride in that steadiness. His wife teases him that nothing rattles him. He believes that too, until the night his younger brother is badly injured.

It happens on an ordinary evening. He is finishing a shift when his phone vibrates repeatedly in his locker. At first he ignores it, assuming it is family chatter in the group thread. When he finally looks, he sees a string of missed calls from his mother and a short message from a cousin: there has been a crash. His brother is involved. He remembers the sudden drop in his stomach and the absurdly practical thought that someone should have told him whether it is head trauma, chest trauma, or both. He drives to the hospital much too fast, rehearsing interventions in his head as if knowledge can bargain with reality.

When he arrives, he is not allowed into the trauma bay right away. That helpless waiting becomes the part he returns to most often later. He can hear the clipped voices, the rolling wheels, the monitor alarms behind the doors. He knows exactly what those sounds usually mean. When he finally sees his brother, there is blood in his hairline, one side of his face swollen beyond recognition, tubes everywhere. He notices details he wishes he did not: the mottled color of his skin, the stiffness of one hand, the smell of antiseptic over something raw and human. He stands there as a brother, but his mind keeps sliding into paramedic mode, scanning, estimating, predicting. He hates himself for doing it.

His brother survives, but with a long, uncertain recovery. In the weeks that follow, he becomes the family's translator, explaining scans and procedures to his parents, answering calls from relatives overseas, speaking in calm sentences while something inside him feels constantly electrified. At the hospital he is composed. At home he is not. He lies awake listening for his phone, afraid of another call. When he does sleep, he wakes suddenly with the image of his brother's face in the trauma bay, or with the sound of unseen monitors. His wife finds him on the couch at 3 a.m., staring at nothing, still in yesterday's clothes.

He returns to work quickly, telling himself that routine will help. Instead, the ambulance feels different. Certain dispatches make his chest tighten before he even arrives. Motor vehicle collisions are the worst. If the patient is a man around his brother's age, he feels a surge of dread so sharp it almost blurs his vision. He still performs well-his hands know what to do-but afterward he sits in the rig longer than usual, replaying pieces of the call and comparing every injury to his brother's. He starts volunteering for other types of runs when he can, pretending it is about fairness in scheduling.

At home, his world narrows. He drives longer routes to avoid the intersection where his brother was hit. Family gatherings, once noisy and comforting, now exhaust him. He cannot bear the way people recount the accident in fragments, each person adding some new horrifying detail. When his mother starts crying, he leaves the room under the pretense of taking a work call. His wife notices he startles when their children drop something heavy in the kitchen. She notices that he sits facing the door in restaurants and scans the room without seeming aware of it. When she asks what is wrong, he tells her he is just tired.

He is also angrier than he used to be. Small things ignite him: traffic, a late bill, his son forgetting his school bag. The anger frightens him because it arrives so fast. He is ashamed after, especially when he sees his children go quiet around him. Sometimes his wife reaches for him in bed and he goes rigid before he realizes what he is doing. He misses the easy affection they used to have, but closeness now feels like one more demand on a system already stretched too tight.

What troubles him most is that he no longer trusts his own mind. He has flash-like moments in the middle of the day-glimpses of the trauma bay, his brother's swollen face, the doors closing. He can be stocking supplies at work or standing in line for coffee, and suddenly he is back there, heart pounding, jaw clenched, as if his body has not learned that the event is over. He tells himself other people have it worse. He tells himself he should be stronger, especially given his job. Yet beneath that is a quieter fear: that the one emergency he could not manage was the one that happened to someone he loves, and that since then he has been living as though disaster is always one phone call away.
